Corrupt spots read as evident: 'ventis et (??)tibus' as fluctibus (waves); 'quae (??) cum' as quatriduanum (four days dead); 'nevit' as flevit; 'omnipotens (??)potentem' as omnipotentem. The clause 'ubicumque legum ... quod minus loqueretur divinitas, sed ... protestatur humanitas' is garbled (probably legunt ... non hoc loqui divinitatem); the bracketed supplement gives the evident sense. The text attributes the Isaiah quotation (Isa. 41:18; 42:5) to Hosea. Some printed references are off (e.g. John 1:2 for 1:1, Exod. 11:26 for 20:26, Col. 1:3 for 2:3, Ps. 116:1 for 116:2); the corrected Exodus reference is given.

Several readings are evidently misprints and have been translated as intended: 'cum docuisse' as 'eum docuisse'; 'num non credent' as 'ne non credant'; 'Et tu cognoscas' as 'Et ut cognoscas'; 'ad quos elegi eos' as 'ad quod'; 'respondit Dominus' taken as the reply [the answer came] in the psalm. The phrase 'cognoscant quod sit videre Filii' seems corrupt and is rendered tentatively. The quotation of 2 Cor. 1:19-20 is garbled in the text ('non fuit in illo est et non, sed est in illo fuit') and is rendered as closely as sense allows. Several scripture references in the edition are inaccurate (e.g. Ps. XXXIII for Ps. 23, Joan. XX, 38 for John 14:10, II Cor. VI, 19 for 1 Cor. 6:19, Matth. XVI, 38 for 26:38, Ps. LII, 9 for Ps. 32:9); corrected references are given. 'Portate Deum' (carry God) follows the Old Latin reading of 1 Cor. 6:20. Scanning errors silently corrected (confossus = confessus, loculus = locutus, Si ta = Si tu, etc.). Several of the edition's citations are wrong and are corrected in the English: 'I Cor. XIII, 13' is 2 Cor. 13:13; 'II Thessal. XXXV' is 2 Thess. 3:5; Matt. 1:18 (printed 28), Matt. 1:21 (printed 25), Luke 5:21 (printed 26), 1 Cor. 2:11 (printed II). 'ad incredulitatem inseparabilis Trinitatis' is odd; perhaps read 'ad credulitatem' ('to [bring about] belief in'). The 'consuming fire' quotation is attributed to Isaiah though it is from Deuteronomy/Hebrews. 'et est Trinitas Deus laudatur' seems corrupt; translated as if 'ut Trinitas Deus laudetur'. In 'qui etiam Deum ... misisse' the sense is that the Spirit sent God the Son, which is the author's argument. The text's own attributions are kept where they differ from the usual ones (e.g. 1 Tim. 1:11 cited 'to Titus'; Jer. 17:22 cited 'in Isaiah'; 2 Thess. 2:16 cited as 1 Thess.). Several references in the edition are off by a verse or two; corrected numbers are given where certain. 3 Kgs 19:11 reads 'Spiritus sanctus, et fortis' where the Vulgate has 'spiritus grandis et fortis'; translated as given. 'Spiritus fortitudinis in viis ejus' has no reference in the text and could not be identified with certainty. The sentence 'and what is above the world, he filled the Lord himself' is awkward in the Latin and may be corrupt. Scanning errors read as intended: 'ex equa it' = ex aqua et, 'reguum' = regnum, 'Quo ibe ab' = Quo ibo a, 'nd' = ad, 'restris' = vestris. The edition cites John 14:16 for 'I am the way, the truth, and the life'; the verse is John 14:6. It cites 1 Cor. 'Xx', 17, evidently 10:17. 'Cos' is read as 'eos', 'unos panis' as 'unus panis'. 'Quam memoravimus' refers to a saying not quoted in this stretch, presumably mentioned earlier in the work.

nodes.text: A SUMMARY OF THE FAITH AGAINST THE ARIAN HERETICS,
IN WHICH THE EQUALITY OF THE THREE DIVINE PERSONS IS CLEARLY PROVED BY A GREAT MANY PASSAGES OF HOLY SCRIPTURE AND BY ARGUMENTS. BY AN UNKNOWN BUT VERY ANCIENT AUTHOR.

This is the chief reason the heretics go wrong: they either do not know, or do not want to notice, that in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person but two substances, God from God the Father, and man from a human mother. And what the Lord himself says of himself according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, they assign to the divinity, such as this: 'The Father is greater than I' (John 14:28), or this: 'Jesus, tired from the journey' (John 4:6), or this: 'He wept for Lazarus' (John 11:35), or other things of this kind that are read. If they would notice that saying of the Apostle: 'God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself' (2 Cor. 5:19), or that of the Gospel: 'The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14), they would not hesitate, as was said above, to confess that in one person there are two substances. And where they hear it said, 'The Father is greater than I,' they would take it according to the humanity; but where they hear, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), they would not doubt that it was said according to the divinity, as is given to be understood from his works. For as man he was hungry, to show that his flesh was real; but as God he fed five thousand men from five loaves, to prove himself God by mighty works. As man he was thirsty, but as God he refreshed the Samaritan woman with living water. As man he went up into a boat, but as God he walked on the sea with dry feet. As man he slept in the boat; as God he commanded the winds and waves. As man he wept for Lazarus; as God he raised him from the tomb when he had been dead four days. As man he hung on the cross; as God he gave paradise to the thief from the cross. As man he suffered and tasted death; as God he raised himself from the dead. If they would discern these and similar things wisely, and assign to each substance what is its own, they could easily keep the course of the right faith, and would not heap insults on his divinity in return for his benefits, the things which he took up or suffered in the form of a servant to redeem us; and wherever they read in the Scriptures something said according to the humanity that would make it lesser, [they would understand that] it is not the divinity that says this, but the humanity that declares it on account of the dispensation of the flesh it assumed. For we, just as we read that he is God, so nowhere do we read of a greater or lesser God, nor ought we to believe [it] with a devout mind. But [the heretic] still persists, and says: 'It cannot be that the son should not be believed less than the father, since he is known to be from the father.' He is deceived by the custom of human generation, so that because he is called son he is believed less than the father. Among men a father begets a son who is less for this reason, that he himself too was begotten less than his father. Therefore as the son grows, the father grows old; and when the father dies, the son is seen to succeed, and sometimes becomes better and more powerful than the father. With God it is not so; for where the divinity cannot grow or grow old, it is fitting that love should have a son who is equal, since fullness cannot have [one] greater. And so the perfect begot the perfect, the almighty the almighty, the full the full; and since he had no increase of age, he could not beget one who was less; but I know that the Son is wholly such as the Father is, as he himself says: 'He who sees me sees the Father also' (John 14:9); and elsewhere: 'He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him' (John 5:23). But perhaps because you hear 'sent', you think him less. I ask you, do you believe the Son is God, or not? Without doubt you will answer, God; for even if you wanted to deny it, you would be refuted by the holy Scriptures, as the Apostle says: 'Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever' (Rom. 9:5). And John in his Epistle: 'That we may be,' he says, 'in his true Son, who is true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20). And Thomas: 'My God,' he says, 'and my Lord' (John 20:28). And Melchizedek the high priest: 'Blessed be Abraham,' he says, 'by God most high, who created heaven and earth' (Gen. 14:19). You see that not merely God, but God most high, is attested by the words of Melchizedek. The prophet Hosea too is a witness, saying: 'Establishing heaven and creating the earth, I am the Lord your God, whose hands created all the host of heaven' (Isa. 41:18; 42:5). If then the Son is God, or rather because he is God, since all things were made through him, and not only not less but God most high, I ask you whether God is everywhere, or perhaps in a place? Since it is impious to deny that God is everywhere, I beg you, where was he sent? But understand the sending of the Son as his incarnation, as the Apostle himself explains: 'God sent,' he says, 'his Son, made of a woman, made under the law' (Gal. 4:4). Then we read of him in the prophet: 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord' (Jer. 23:24). And the Evangelist of the same: 'Of his fullness,' he says, 'we have all received' (John 1:16). And if he himself fills all things, where was he sent, by whose majesty all things are full? But perhaps you still say, as the fleshly understanding has it, that between the begetting Father and the begotten Son there could not but have been some interval. Intervals make hours, hours mark time; and so, if you set time before the Son, you do not confess that all things were made through him. And where is that saying: 'All things were made through him' (ibid., 3)? Indeed, I answer according to your own proposition, you who say that the Father was at some time without the Son. We read likewise in the Apostle: 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor. 1:24); and the Lord himself says of himself: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). If then the Father was without the Son, as you say, he was without power, he was without wisdom, he was without life, he was without truth. But since the Father must never be believed to have been without these, it befits your salvation to confess, according to the catholic faith, that the Son is co-eternal and equal with the Father: for his power too is read to be everlasting, as the Apostle says: 'Also his everlasting power and divinity' (Rom. 1:20). Likewise of truth, as the Psalmist says: 'And the truth of the Lord remains for ever' (Ps. 116:1). They are also accustomed, by way of slander, to raise this as a question: 'The Father is so much greater,' they say, 'that he is always named in the first place.' Even if he were always named in the first place, it would seem quite fitting, since the Son is from him, not he from the Son. Yet so that you may recognise the equality, hear where in the Scriptures the Son is even named first. John the evangelist says: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:2). By 'Word' he certainly indicated the Son. And the Apostle to the Ephesians: 'Do you not know that no fornicator or unclean person has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God?' (Eph. 5:5). See, here too the Son is named in the first place. And to the Galatians: 'Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father' (Gal. 1:1). And to the Thessalonians: 'Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us' (2 Thess. 2:15). To the Corinthians: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all' (2 Cor. 13:13). And the Lord himself says: 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). He does not say, 'The Father and I.' And elsewhere: 'He who sees me sees the Father also' (John 14:9). And again: 'He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him' (John 5:23). See how often the Son is named in the first place! But since there is equality in the Father and the Son, being named before or after can bring no prejudice to either, for there is no difference where the divinity in both is equal. We read it so for this reason, that human speech cannot manage otherwise than to name one and then the other. See, so that you may recognise that nothing there is greater and nothing less, the question about the Father being named first has fallen away; for where there is one substance, one deity, and an incorporeal immensity, no disparity or difference is to be supposed. For where one God is believed, greater and lesser are excluded. Unity knows no number, and equality admits no steps, as it is written: 'You shall not go up by steps to my altar' (Exod. 20:26). And therefore let [the heretic] put away contention and hold with the catholic faith the inseparable Trinity, joined without mingling, distinguished without separation, for the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are God full and one. For reason itself teaches that one admits neither a later nor an earlier; he who alone is cannot have comparison or separation; he who is full cannot be less, for nothing can be added to perfection nor taken away. Let three persons then be believed, but not three substances; three properties, but not three powers. Thus there is one eternity without beginning, just as there is one majesty without end: the Father without an author, the Son without time, the Holy Spirit without a greater. For we catholics say that our Lord God Jesus Christ is both less than the Father and equal: less because of the humanity assumed, since being in the form of God he deigned to put on the form of a servant; but we call him equal because of the everlasting deity, by which the Son, existing from the Father, is also co-eternal with the Father. Why then do they not confess with us that he is equal, when we do not deny with them that he is less? Especially since we read both in the holy Scriptures, as the Evangelist says: 'Therefore,' he says, 'the Jews sought to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God' (John 5:18). See, the impiety of the Jews calls him equal, and a Christian is not afraid to call him less. And elsewhere the same Evangelist says: 'He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him' (ibid., 23). For equal honour is shown only to equals. And in another place the same says: 'As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he will' (ibid., 21). Hear him saying: 'As the Father, so also the Son.' Hear him saying: 'To whom he will,' and recognise that he is equal to the Father and of his own power; and do not call God less, for nowhere in the holy Scriptures do we read of a greater God or a lesser. As he himself says to Philip: 'He who sees me sees the Father also' (John 14:9). And: 'Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does the same' (John 5:19). Or that: 'The Word was God' (John 1:1). And the Apostle, as we have mentioned: 'Who is,' he says, 'God over all, blessed for ever' (Rom. 9:5). And the Apostle: 'Who, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God' (Phil. 2:6). Why this? Because no one seizes except what he does not have. So he who had equality did not think of it as by robbery; but what the rebel angel wanted to take by robbery, Christ possessed by nature. And that he is true God, hear blessed John saying in his Epistle: 'And let us be,' he says, 'in his true Son Jesus Christ: this is the true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20). You hear 'true God', and you presume to call him less, and do not confess him equal? The blessed Apostle also says to Titus: 'Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God' (Titus 2:13). I do not know with what face he can be called less whom the Apostle professes to be the great God. This faithless error is also accustomed to say that where in the Scriptures we read 'the only God', or 'the only Most High', or 'the only wise', this is not said of the Trinity but ought to be taken of the Father alone. How absurd it is to think so may be proved by this one testimony. For the Apostle says: 'Made known to the only wise God' (Rom. 16:26). They do not understand that he did not say, 'to the only wise Father', but 'to the only wise God', which is the Trinity. For when they assign this to the Father alone, they blasphemously make the Son unwise. And how does the Apostle say that he is the wisdom of God, if the Father alone is wise, when no one can be wise except through his wisdom? And where is that which the same Apostle declares to the Colossians about Christ Jesus: 'In whom,' he says, 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Col. 1:3)? From this let them recognise how foolish is what they put forward, and wherever they read something similar, let them not assign it to one person but to the blessed Trinity, which alone is the supreme and true God. For of the Holy Spirit too the Apostle says thus: 'To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit' (1 Cor. 12:8). If then through the Holy Spirit, as is true, both the word of wisdom and of knowledge is given, how can it be ascribed to the person of the Father alone that he alone is wise, unless, as has been said, these things belong to the co-eternal Trinity? They are also accustomed to say that the Son is less because he is visible, while the Father is invisible. They do not understand that the Son too is not visible in the substance of his deity, but only in the man assumed, who is also called Christ. For the Son of God, that is the Word, who was in the beginning God with God, through whom all things were made, could not be seen in his own substance, just as the Father could not in his. But I ask, without offence to him, the very man who says that the Son of God was seen, whether he confesses his own soul to be visible or invisible; and when he says invisible, as is indeed true, let it be said to him: 'If a creature, that is your soul, is invisible, being of course a creature of God, how could the creator of the universe be visible?' But he put on flesh, which could be seen, for this reason: because the deity could not be seen by man. By this flesh the Father is greater: equal to the Word, greater than the flesh; equal to him through whom he made us, greater than him who was made for our sake. Now that the Son is God, although the many testimonies set out above plainly teach it, I have nevertheless thought that a few more should be added. In Genesis it is written: 'God created the heaven' (Gen. 1:1), and the Evangelist certainly confirms that all things were created by the Son (John 1:3). Likewise there follows there: 'God created man after his own image and likeness' (Gen. 1:27). See, recognise God here, because he himself also created man. And Isaiah says of John, the forerunner of the Lord: 'Make straight the paths of our God' (Isa. 40:3). Of what God, if not of the Son, whom we do not doubt to have come in the flesh? And a little after: 'Strengthen the slack hands, and make firm the weak knees. Say to the faint-hearted: See, your God will come in strength and will save you, and then the eyes of the blind shall be opened' (Isa. 35:3). This we know to have been fulfilled in the coming of Christ. The Psalmist too says: 'All the nations, whomever you have made, shall come and worship before you; you are wonderful and do wonderful things; you alone are God' (Ps. 85:9). I do not think anyone is so impious as to deny that the Son of God both did wonderful things and created all the nations, unless perhaps the Jews. And elsewhere Isaiah, when he announces the coming of Christ through a virgin, says among other things: 'And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God' (Isa. 9:6). And the blessed Apostle too: 'For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ' (2 Cor. 5:10). And so that you may recognise that Christ is God, he says thus elsewhere: 'We shall all stand before the judgement seat of God (Rom. 14:10). As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me.' Certainly he says this of Christ, who we believe will come to judge the living and the dead. The Psalmist, giving voice to the angels when Christ had ascended into heaven, says: 'Lift up your gates, you princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the king of glory shall come in' (Ps. 23:7). And when they asked who this king of glory was, [the answer] came: 'The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord of hosts; he is the king of glory' (ibid. 8, 10). And lest perhaps they think this was said of the Father, as they understand many things absurdly, let them hear the Apostle agreeing with this verse: 'For if they had known,' he says, 'they would never have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Cor. 2:8). Since by the present testimonies as well as the earlier ones, which have been drawn from the holy Scriptures, the Son is shown to be God, I wonder why some do not fear to blaspheme by calling him less, when God is nowhere at all read to be less, except, as has been said, on account of the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, in which he was not only made lower than the angels, but is also found to be younger than his mother, as we have already said. According to this rule, then, believe that there are two substances in Christ, true God and true man. According to the man he is subjected to death; according to God he is known to be the author of life, as blessed Peter says: 'You asked for a murderer to be granted to you, but you killed the author of life' (Acts 3:14). According to the man: 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' (Matt. 26:38); according to God: 'I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself' (John 10:18). From this too they are accustomed to take an occasion for slander, that the Lord said in the Gospel: 'The Son cannot do anything else except what he has seen the Father doing' (John 5:19). Carnal understanding, not grasping this, thinks it was said so that he might show that he is from the Father, as being both God and Son, in the way it usually happens among men, as when a father who is a craftsman teaches his son his craft, so that what the son has seen the father working at, he may imitate quite particularly. How absurd it is to believe this of God the Father almighty, who is incorporeal, invisible, beyond reckoning and immeasurable, anyone who has sound eyes of the heart can plainly recognise. For those who think so must be asked: By whom was this world that we see made? Certainly they will not deny that it was by the Son, the Evangelist bearing witness and saying: 'All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made' (John 1:3). Let them say, then, where the Son saw the Father previously making another world, so that afterwards he might create this one in the same way; especially since with the power of God to have willed is to have created, as we read: 'He spoke, and they were made' (Ps. 32:9). But let them take away the veil from their heart and learn to believe that the Son is in the Father and the Father is in the Son: because the divinity, wholly present everywhere, of the Father as much as of the Son as of the Holy Spirit, can nowhere be without itself, as he himself says: 'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' (John 14:10); and let them recognise what the seeing of the Son is, namely that there is one substance, one power, one glory. Let nothing there be believed greater, and nothing less. For if we earthly men accomplish what we wish to do with the body by first sending ahead the prompting of reflection in our mind, with wisdom carrying it out, and in a certain way, a plan having been born in our mind, first do inwardly in the heart what we arrange to do, all of which, however, one mind brings about inseparably, without any division of the faculties: how does God the Father not accomplish all things in one will and one operation with God the Son, who is his wisdom abiding in him, since he is, as we have often said, the wisdom and power of the Father? Nor does the Father do some things and the Son others; but the very things the Father does, these the Son also does, as he himself testifies: 'Whatever the Father does,' he says, 'these same things the Son also does likewise' (John 5:19). But he said, 'The Son cannot do anything of himself except what he has seen the Father doing' (ibid.), for this reason: so that we may know and believe that the Son is from the Father, and not from himself or from elsewhere, but co-eternal with the Father, because the Father too always exists perfect in himself, and nothing was ever lacking to him or added to him. For if at some time, as the Arians blasphemously say, the Father was without the Son, then the Father was imperfect, then he was without the Word, and, as we have already mentioned, he was without wisdom, without power, without life, without justice, without truth: because the Son is known, according to the Scriptures, to be all these forms of the divinity. But since it is blasphemous to say that the Father was ever without these powers, this is just, this is fitting, that you confess the Son co-eternal and co-equal with the Father. For if, when God speaks in our hearts, he speaks in a wonderful way without sound, how do you suppose he can speak to his Son, who is his Word? Think, then, in this way: that he spoke to the Son incorporeally, because he also begot the Son incorporeally. For he did not teach him as though he had begotten him untaught. But to have taught him is this: to have begotten him taught and knowing. And this is [the meaning of] 'The Father taught me' (John 8:28), that is, the Father begot me knowing. But how can the Son do nothing of himself, of whom the Prophet testifies and says: 'But our God is in heaven above, and on earth he has done all things whatsoever he willed' (Ps. 113:11)? But if perhaps you are going to say that this was said of the Father, go back to the Evangelist saying of the Son that 'all things were made through him, without him nothing was made' (John 1:3). It is he also who speaks to Moses: 'Go,' he says, 'say to the children of Israel: The God of your fathers has sent me to you' (Exod. 3:13). When he answered and said, 'Tell me your name, lest they not believe me,' after this God, adding, said to him: 'Go, say to the children of Israel: I am who am, and he who is has sent me to you' (ibid. 14). And lest you take this as said of the Father, hear the blessed Apostle agreeing with this passage and in a certain way expounding this very testimony, to the Corinthians: 'The Son of God,' he says, 'who was preached among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not "is" and "is not" in him, but in him was "is". For as many as are the promises of God, in him is [the] "is"' (2 Cor. 1:19-20). Hear Paul agreeing with Moses, and do not disagree with the catholic faith. For if you ask the catholic Church what the Father is, it says God; but it also says the Son is God, and it also says the Holy Spirit is God; and yet it does not say three gods, lest it be likened to the gentiles, who, deceived by their error, invent many gods. But we shall believe Scripture, of the New as well as the Old Testament, which says that God is one: and if one is greater and another less, as the Arians say, he cannot be called one; inequality excludes unity. Notice, then, how we believe [them] three and one. Equality of powers makes the unity, the property of the persons makes the Trinity. You have heard how he himself taught that his equality with the Father is to be understood: 'I and the Father,' he says, 'are one' (John 10:30). 'One' is one thing, 'are' another. For when he says 'are', he signifies the persons. 'We are one', that is, we are justice, and the same wisdom, undivided power, equal glory. Since this is so, let dissension be removed and the faith be held entire. They also say: 'The Father is greater for this reason, that he is immortal.' They must be asked whether they confess that the Son is mortal in the substance of his deity. If they say so, how contrary to reason they speak anyone can recognise who does not doubt that even the human soul is immortal. But this must be said to them: that he is said to have suffered and died according to the flesh. For according to the divinity, in which he always existed and created all things, he remains immortal. They also say that he is visible; let those who say this recognise how absurd it is, since not even the human soul can be visible, how much less God in his own substance? But he assumed flesh, which could be seen, for this reason: because the deity could not be beheld by bodily eyes. Let these things said for the present about the equality of the Father and the Son suffice for now. For concerning the equality of the works of the Trinity, that is of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, we shall show it a little later from the holy Scriptures, the Lord granting. Now, however, a few testimonies out of many must be set down about the deity of the Holy Spirit, whom the heretics are said not only to assert is less, but even to deny altogether is God. Let them hear a few things about the deity of the Holy Spirit. In Genesis the divine word says: 'The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters' (Gen. 1:2). This is the eminence of power, not the poverty of need. And in the Gospel: 'God is Spirit, and those who worship must worship in spirit and truth' (John 4:24). And lest perhaps you understand this as said of the Father and not of the Holy Spirit, hear what follows: 'The Spirit breathes where he wills' (John 3:8). Hear 'where he wills', so that you may not doubt that he is under his own power. And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: 'There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all' (1 Cor. 12:4-6). And so that you may recognise that the Spirit himself is named Lord and God, hear further down how he concludes: 'To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit' (ibid. 8-9), and the rest. And he concludes thus: 'But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, dividing to each as he wills' (ibid. 11). He who dispenses divine gifts as he wills knows no law of a superior. Recognise at last that he who divides as he wills is proved to be subject to no one, but is known to be under his own power. For will descends from supreme power, which no authority contradicts. And to the Hebrews he speaks similarly of the distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will. And who this distributor and divider is he shows plainly to the Romans, saying: 'To each as God has divided the measure of faith' (Rom. 12:3). And to the Corinthians: 'Do you not know,' he says, 'that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor. 3:16)? But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him' (ibid. 17). And who this God is whose temple he forbids to be violated, hear in what follows: 'Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit' (1 Cor. 6:19)? And who this Holy Spirit is whose temple we are, he shows, concluding thus: 'Glorify,' he says, 'and carry God in your body' (ibid. 20). Recognise that the Holy Spirit is plainly God, and stop blaspheming. And in the Acts of the Apostles blessed Peter speaks thus to Ananias, who had vowed an offering to God and afterwards proved undevoted: 'Who compelled you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God' (Acts 5:3-4). See, here too the witness of blessed Peter makes it most evident that he is God. Likewise there: 'The Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have chosen them' (Acts 13:2). And blessed Paul said in the same book: 'Take heed,' he says, 'to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has set you as apostles, to rule the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood' (Acts 20:28). And who it is that sets apart and sends the apostles, the same Paul declares to the Corinthians, saying: 'And God,' he says, 'has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers' (1 Cor. 12:28), and so on. See where he has shown that the Holy Spirit is God more clearly than light: the one he calls the Holy Spirit in the Acts of the Apostles, he plainly confessed to the Corinthians to be God. For the same vessel of election says to the Jews: 'Well did the Holy Spirit prophesy about you through the mouth of Isaiah the prophet' (Acts 28:25). And who this Holy Spirit is who spoke in the prophets, blessed David expresses, saying: 'I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me' (Ps. 84:9). And in the Acts: 'So that the Scripture might be fulfilled,' he says, 'which God foretold through the mouth of his prophets' (Acts 3:18). Here too recognise that he plainly declares the one who spoke through the mouth of the prophets to be God, just as Zechariah also says in the Gospel: 'Blessed,' he says, 'be the God of Israel, for he has visited and brought about the redemption of his people' (Luke 1:68), and a little after, he says: 'As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets' (ibid. 70). You recognise that the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of the prophets, is the Lord God, which not even the impious Jews deny. If he were not God, he would not be joined with the Father and the Son in baptism in the one name of the deity, as it is written where the Lord himself laid down the rule of baptism: 'Go,' he says, 'baptise all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 28:19). This testimony alone ought to suffice the heretics against [their] unbelief in the inseparable Trinity, since not even they dare to baptise otherwise, lest they seem to corrupt the Lord's rule. And where one name is spoken, there greater and lesser are excluded. And in the second [letter] to the Corinthians: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all' (2 Cor. 13:13). That you may recognise that the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one substance and deity, hear Isaiah the prophet saying: 'Who weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers' (Isa. 40:12). For we also find in the Scriptures the Holy Spirit called, in the singular, a finger, as in that [passage] in the Gospel where he says: 'If I cast out demons by the finger of God' (Luke 11:20); which another evangelist makes clear, saying: 'If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God' (Matt. 12:28). And Pharaoh's magicians, overcome by the divine signs, say: 'It is the finger of God' (Exod. 8:19). At Pentecost, which the Jews kept even before the coming of Christ, Moses received the tablets inscribed by the finger of God, that is, by the Spirit; and [the Spirit,] who then in the stone tablets prefigured the very hard hearts of the Jews, after the Lord's Ascension deigned to appear visibly on tablets of flesh, that is, in the hearts of the disciples, in the very form of fire in which he appeared to Moses in the desert, of whom we believe Isaiah says: 'Our God is a consuming fire' (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29). And since we read that no one knows the thoughts of men except God, how is the Holy Spirit not God, who is known to know not only the things that are in man but also those that are in God? As the Apostle says: 'For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God' (1 Cor. 2:10); and a little after: 'So no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God' (ibid. 11). But perhaps someone says that he is lesser for this reason, that he is read to have been sent. And what will he say when he reads in Isaiah the prophet, in the person of Christ speaking: 'The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit' (Isa. 48:16)? And elsewhere: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach release to the poor, and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord' (Isa. 61:1), and so on. And that you may know plainly that it was said of the Lord, the Evangelist says: 'When the Lord Jesus had come into the synagogue, the book of Isaiah the prophet was given to him, and opening it he found written: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me' (Luke 4:17), and the rest that we said above. And after this: 'He rolled up the book,' he says, 'and gave it to the attendant, and said: Today this scripture has been fulfilled among you' (ibid. 20). Is he to be believed to be sent who is known to be everywhere? As the Psalmist says: 'Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face' (Ps. 138:7)? But just as the sending of the Son is declared [to be] the incarnation, [so his sending is declared] when he deigned to make himself known either in the form of a dove, or in fire, or by taking on various signs of this kind. How then is he to be believed lesser, who is shown to have sent even God, who, like himself, is equal to the Father, for our forgiveness? And not only to have sent [him], as we recalled was said through Isaiah, but also to have created [him] according to the flesh, as you have in the Gospel that the angel said to Mary: 'The Holy Spirit,' he says, 'will come upon you, the power of the Most High will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35), and so on. For Christ was conceived not by begetting, but by the command and blessing of the Holy Spirit, as another evangelist also says: 'She was found,' he says, 'to have [a child] in her womb from the Holy Spirit' (Matt. 1:18). The prophets, moreover, often say, as we have already recalled, 'Thus says the Lord.' And who this Lord is the prophet Micaiah plainly shows when he speaks to Ahab, saying: 'If you return safe from the battle, God has not spoken in me' (3 Kgs. 22:28). And who this God is who spoke in the prophets, Paul the apostle shows when he says to the Jews: 'Well,' he says, 'did the Holy Spirit prophesy about you through the mouth of Isaiah the prophet' (Acts 28:25): 'Go,' he says, 'blind the heart of this people' (Isa. 6:10), and so on. Yet the heretics must be asked whose offence is greater: his who sins against the Father, or his who [sins] against the Holy Spirit, whom they say is not God. And when they say that the offence of him who sins against the Father is greater, they must be asked again whether the children of Israel sinned against the Father or against another. When they answer that they sinned against the Father, they must be asked again whether their sins were forgiven them. Certainly they will not deny it, since we read that they turned to God and their sins were forgiven them. Then they must be asked to explain how they understand what was said by the Lord: 'Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come' (Matt. 12:32). If he is not God, why should an offence against him be said by the Lord to be so grave? Again they must be asked whether the children of Israel were defiant towards God or not. When they do not deny it, since they cannot, it must be said to them: how do they take what blessed Stephen reproaches the Jews with, saying: 'You have always resisted the Holy Spirit, and have always been defiant towards him, as your fathers also were' (Acts 7:51)? Hear also [what is written] to the Thessalonians, where he both puts the Holy Spirit first in place and calls him Lord, saying: 'But may the Lord direct your hearts in the love of God and the patience of Christ' (2 Thess. 3:5). Note carefully that here the Holy Spirit is prayed to, to direct the hearts of believers in the love of God and in the patience of Christ. They must also be asked which is greater, the heavens or the powers of the heavens? And when they say without doubt the powers of the heavens, it must be said to them: so far is the Holy Spirit from being lesser, rather he is supreme, that while the heavens are said to have been created by the word of the Lord, the powers of the heavens [were created] by the Holy Spirit. Take further [a passage] where the Holy Spirit is plainly described as creator. Job says: 'The divine Spirit who made me' (Job 33:4). And in one short verse he has shown him to be both divine and creator: when he calls him divine, he shows him to be both God and creator. As David too says: 'Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth' (Ps. 103:30). They must also be asked whether a creature can be everywhere or not. And when they answer that it cannot be everywhere, as is indeed true, it must be said without doubt: the Holy Spirit, who is described as being everywhere, is God and not a creature. Of whom, as has already been said, the Prophet, in awe of his omnipotence, says: 'Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face' (Ps. 138:7)? Recognise then that there is no place where the omnipotence of the Holy Spirit is not shown to be present. Likewise they must be asked whether anyone besides God can forgive sins; and when they answer that no one but God [can], since it is written: 'No one can forgive sins but God alone' (Luke 5:21), it must be said to them that without doubt the Holy Spirit is God, who is known to confer the forgiveness of sins, as the Lord said: 'Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven them' (John 20:22-23). He also, with the Father and the Son, grants forgiveness of sins to the baptised in baptism. Hear also that the Holy Spirit is God, who is frequently joined with the Father and the Son. To the Corinthians, as has already been said: 'The grace,' he says, 'of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all' (2 Cor. 13:13). If he were not God but a creature, as the heretic blasphemously says, he would never be joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, where the salvation of the human race is at stake. For that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, the prophet Isaiah says, as we have already recalled: 'Who weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers' (Isa. 40:12)? In this place he taught thoroughly, by the three fingers, that there is one substance in three persons. Understanding this as said of the Trinity, the Apostle says: 'All things are from him, and through him, and in him are all things' (Rom. 11:36), that is, all things are held together by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Likewise the same Apostle says to the Corinthians: 'God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, who has shone in our hearts [to give] the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus' (2 Cor. 4:6). In this place the Trinity is most clearly understood. In 'God, who said that light should shine out of darkness,' the Holy Spirit is recognised; and where he says, 'the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God,' the Father is understood; but in that where he says, 'in the face of Christ Jesus,' the Son is designated. Hear further that the Trinity abides in unity and unity in Trinity, as the voices of the angels and archangels declare in Isaiah, where the Seraphim are written to sing the hymn, 'Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth' (Isa. 6:3): it concludes not with three holy ones but with one thrice holy, by saying 'Lord God Sabaoth', that is, so that you may understand three persons and one God. They do not say it once, lest you believe in singularity; not twice, lest you exclude the Holy Spirit; not 'holy Lords Sabaoth', lest you confess three gods in the manner of the pagans. But they say, 'Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Sabaoth', and [so] the Trinity is praised as God, who is the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That he is God, whoever has healthy eyes of the heart will easily be able to prove from the equality of their operations, as we shall show in what follows. As the Father saves, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'Save us, our God, and gather us from the nations' (Ps. 105:47). Of the Son: 'The Son of Man came to save what was lost' (Luke 19:10); and elsewhere: 'For he will save his people from their sins' (Matt. 1:21). Of the Holy Spirit, to Titus: 'He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit' (Titus 3:5). As the Father strengthens, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Esther of the Father: 'Strengthen me, King, and God of the two' (Esther 14:12). Of the Son, the Apostle: 'I give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, who strengthened me and judged me faithful' (1 Tim. 1:12). Of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel: 'And the boy grew and was strengthened by the Holy Spirit' (Luke 1:80). The Father gives life, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: 'As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills' (John 5:21). Of the Holy Spirit in the Letter of the apostle Peter: 'Put to death in the flesh, but made alive by the Spirit' (1 Pet. 3:18). And the apostle Paul: 'The letter,' he says, 'kills, but the Spirit gives life' (2 Cor. 3:6). And in the Gospel: 'It is the Spirit who gives life, for the flesh profits nothing' (John 6:64). As the Father sets free, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'God most high, their deliverer' (Ps. 77:35). Of the Son in the Gospel: 'If he sets you free, you will be free indeed, and the truth will set you free' (John 8:36, 32). Of the Holy Spirit: 'The Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death' (Rom. 8:2). The Father chooses, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, the Apostle: 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who chose us before the foundation of the world' (Eph. 1:3-4). Of the Son: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you' (John 15:16). Of the Holy Spirit in the Acts: 'So when they had fasted and prayed, the Holy Spirit said to them: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work for which I have chosen them' (Acts 13:2). The Father is called Creator, so is the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, the Apostle: 'What is the dispensation of the mystery hidden in God, who created all things' (Eph. 3:9). Of the Son, to the Colossians: 'For by him all things were created, and all things hold together in him' (Col. 1:16-17); and in the Gospel: 'All things were made through him' (John 1:3). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: 'He both saw and numbered and measured all things; he himself created them through the Holy Spirit' (Ecclus. 1:9); and in the Psalm: 'Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created' (Ps. 103:30); and elsewhere: 'By the Spirit of his mouth all their power' (Ps. 32:6). As the Father foretold, so did the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'But God, who foretold that his Christ would suffer, has fulfilled [it]' (Acts 3:18). So of the Son, in the Gospel, the angel said to the women: 'Go and announce to the brothers that he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he foretold to you' (Mark 16:7). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Acts, Peter: 'The scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David' (Acts 1:16). The Father is great, so is the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'Great is our God and worthy of praise' (Ps. 47:2). Of the Son, to Titus: 'Awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God, our Saviour Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13). Of the Holy Spirit, in Kings, the Lord says to Elijah: 'Behold, the Lord passed by, and the Holy Spirit, and strong' (3 Kgs 19:11). As there is love of the Father, so of the Son, so also of the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'But the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ overflowed, and the love of our God' (1 Tim. 1:14). Of the Son: 'For the love of Christ urges us on' (2 Cor. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit: 'What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in the love of the Spirit?' (1 Cor. 4:21); and elsewhere: 'The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us' (Rom. 5:5). The Father gives eternal life, so does the Son, so does the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, in the Epistle of John: 'For God will give us eternal life' (1 John 5:11). Of the Son, in the Gospel: 'My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life' (John 10:27-28). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Galatians: 'He who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit' (Gal. 6:8). As the Father gives peace, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding' (Phil. 4:7). Of the Son, in the Gospel: 'My peace I leave to you' (John 14:27). Of the Holy Spirit: 'But the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace' (Rom. 8:6). The Father reveals, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, to the Galatians: 'To reveal his Son in me' (Gal. 1:16). Of the Son, in the same place: 'For I did not receive it from a man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ' (ibid., 12). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Ephesians: 'Which was not made known to other generations as it has now been revealed to his saints through his Holy Spirit' (Eph. 3:5); and elsewhere: 'For God has revealed [it] to us through the Spirit' (1 Cor. 2:10). As the Father enlightens, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'You will light my lamp, O Lord' (Ps. 17:29). Of the Son, in the Apostle: 'Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will give you light' (Eph. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit, the same Apostle: 'For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts the enlightenment of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus' (2 Cor. 4:6). As the Gospel is said to be of the Father, so of the Son, so also of the Holy Spirit. Of the Father, to Titus: 'Which is according to the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God' (1 Tim. 1:11). Of the Son, to the Romans: 'Whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son' (Rom. 1:9). Of the Holy Spirit, in the epistle of blessed Peter: 'But these things were ministered to you by those who preached the Gospel to you in the Holy Spirit' (1 Pet. 1:12). As the Father has shone, so has the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'My God, enlighten my darkness' (Ps. 17:29). Of the Son, in the Psalm: 'God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us' (Ps. 117:27). Of the Holy Spirit, the Prophet: 'I will no longer hide my face from them, because my spirit has shone upon the whole house of Israel' (Ezek. 39:29). And the Apostle: 'For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, who has shone in our hearts for the enlightenment of the glory of God in the face of God, Christ Jesus' (2 Cor. 4:6). The Father has foreknowledge, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'God, who are the knower of hidden things' (Dan. 13:42). Of the Son: 'From the beginning,' it says, 'Jesus knew who would betray him' (John 6:65). Of the Holy Spirit: 'When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, he will teach you all truth, and will announce to you the things that are to come' (John 16:13). As the Father is said to be everywhere, so is the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord' (Jer. 23:24). Of the Son: 'Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst' (Matt. 18:20); and the Apostle: 'Who ascended above the heavens that he might fill all things' (Eph. 4:10). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: 'The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world' (Wisd. 1:7); and what is above the world, he filled the Lord himself, the founder of the whole world, as we read: 'But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan' (Luke 4:1). And David: 'Where shall I go from your Spirit?' (Ps. 138:7). The Father rebukes, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. Of the Father: 'Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger' (Ps. 6:2). Of the Son: 'I will rebuke you, and set those things before your face' (Ps. 49:21). Of the Spirit: 'When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, he will convict the world of sin' (John 16:8), and the rest. The Father is good, the Son is good, the Holy Spirit is good also. Of the Father: 'Good Father' (John 17:11). Of the Son: 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10:14). Of the Holy Spirit: 'Your good Spirit will lead me in the right way' (Ps. 142:10). As the Father sanctifies and justifies, so does the Son, so also the Holy Spirit. The Apostle: 'But you have been sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God' (1 Cor. 6:11). The Father is called holy, the Son is called holy, the Holy Spirit [is called] holy also. Of the Father, in Leviticus: 'Be holy, for I am holy' (Lev. 11:44). Of the Son, in the Gospel: 'The holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God' (Luke 1:35). Likewise there: 'We know who you are, the holy one of God' (Luke 4:34). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: 'For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit' (Wisd. 1:5). The Father is strong, the Son is strong, the Holy Spirit is strong also. Of the Father: 'God, strong and patient' (Ps. 7:12). Of the Son, in Isaiah: 'And his name will be called strong God' (Isa. 9:6). Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon: 'The spirit of strength in his ways.' The Father works, the Son works, the Holy Spirit [does] this also. Of the Father, to the Philippians: 'For it is God who works in you both to will [and to accomplish]' (Phil. 2:13). Of the Son, in the Gospel: 'I must work the works of him who sent me' (John 9:4). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Corinthians: 'But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills' (1 Cor. 12:11). The Father is power, the Son is power, the Holy Spirit is power also. Of the Father, the Apostle: 'I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes' (Rom. 1:16). Of the Son, the Apostle: 'I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me' (2 Cor. 12:9). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Thessalonians: 'Our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but in the power of the Holy Spirit' (1 Thess. 1:5). The Father is a fountain, the Son is a fountain, the Holy Spirit is a fountain also. Of the Father, Jeremiah: 'They have forsaken the fountain of living water' (Jer. 2:13). Of the Son, in Solomon: 'The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God' (Ecclus. 1:5). Of the Holy Spirit, Isaiah: 'Behold, the name of the Lord coming after a long time, burning in the wrath of his indignation; he will devour the nations, and his Spirit [will be] like a fountain of water drawing along a valley' (Isa. 30:27-28). The Father is love, the Son is love, the Holy Spirit is love also. Of the Father, in the Epistle of John: 'God is love' (1 John 4:16). Of the Son, the Apostle to the Corinthians: 'For the love of Christ urges us on' (2 Cor. 5:14). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle: 'I beseech you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit' (Rom. 15:30). The Father regenerates, the Son regenerates, the Holy Spirit regenerates also. Of the Father, Peter: 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us into the hope of eternal life' (1 Pet. 1:3). Of the Son, in the same place: 'Loving one another from the heart, as reborn through the word of the living God' (ibid., 22-23). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: 'Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven' (John 3:5). The Father raises up, the Son raises up, the Holy Spirit raises up also. Of the Father, in the Acts: 'The God of our fathers, who raised up Jesus, will also raise us up by his power' (Acts 5:30). Of the Son, in the Gospel: 'The Jews came not only on account of Jesus, but to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead' (John 12:9). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle: 'But if his Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead, dwells in you, he will also give life to your mortal bodies on account of his Spirit dwelling in you' (Rom. 8:11). There is grace of God the Father, grace of the Son, and grace of the Holy Spirit also. Of the Father: 'Who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ' (Rom. 7:24-25). Of the Son, to the Corinthians: 'For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sake he became poor, though he was rich' (2 Cor. 8:9). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Acts: 'And those who had come with Peter were astonished that the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles' (Acts 10:45). The Father seals, the Son seals, the Holy Spirit seals also. Of the Father, to the Corinthians: 'And he who sealed you with us in Christ, and who anointed us, is God' (2 Cor. 1:21-22). Of the Son, to the Ephesians: 'Hearing the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, in which you were sealed' (Eph. 1:13). Of the Holy Spirit, in the place cited above: 'Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' (Eph. 4:30). The Father dwells in believers, the Son dwells, the Holy Spirit dwells also. Of the Father, in Isaiah: 'Keep the sabbath day and sanctify it, that I may dwell in your midst' (Jer. 17:22). Of the Son, to the Ephesians: 'That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts' (Eph. 3:17). Of the Holy Spirit: 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (1 Cor. 3:16). The Father searches, the Son searches, the Holy Spirit searches also. Of the Father, in the Psalm: 'God, searching hearts and reins' (Ps. 7:10). Of the Son, in the Apocalypse: 'And all the Churches will know that I am the searcher of heart and reins' (Rev. 2:23). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Apostle: 'The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God' (1 Cor. 2:10). The Father bears witness, the Son bears witness, the Holy Spirit bears witness also. Of the Father, in the Psalm: 'The testimony of God is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones' (Ps. 18:8). Of the Son, to Timothy: 'I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate' (1 Tim. 6:13). Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle: 'He bears witness to our spirit' (Rom. 8:16). The Father shows, the Son shows, the Holy Spirit shows also. Of the Father, to Timothy: 'Whom in his own times the blessed and only mighty one will show' (1 Tim. 6:15). Of the Son, in the Gospel, the Son himself says: 'But I will show you whom you should fear' (Luke 12:5); and: 'I have shown you many good works from my Father' (John 10:32). Of the Holy Spirit, to the Corinthians: 'My preaching was not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the showing of the Spirit' (1 Cor. 2:4). The Father fills, the Son fills, the Holy Spirit fills also. Of the Father, Jeremiah: 'I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord' (Jer. 23:24). Of the Son, in the Apostle: 'But may the Lord fill your hearts and strengthen [them] in every good work and word' (2 Thess. 2:16). And in the Gospel: 'From his fullness we have all received' (John 1:16). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Acts: 'It filled the whole place where the disciples were gathered' (Acts 2:2). And: 'Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan' (Luke 4:1). The Father speaks, the Son speaks, the Holy Spirit speaks also. Of the Father: 'God has spoken in his holy place' (Ps. 59:8). Of the Son: 'While Jesus was speaking to the crowds' (Matt. 12:46). Of the Holy Spirit: 'It is he who speaks in you' (Matt. 10:20). The Father appeared, the Son appeared, the Holy Spirit appeared also. Of the Father, in the Acts: 'The God of glory appeared to our fathers' (Acts 7:2). Of the Son, in the epistle of John: 'For this the Son appeared, that the works of the devil might be destroyed' (1 John 3:8). Of the Holy Spirit, in Job: 'And a spirit appeared before my eyes, and horror rushed upon me' (Job 4:15). The Father is truth, the Son is truth, the Holy Spirit is truth also. Of the Father, in the Psalm: 'You have redeemed me, Lord God of truth' (Ps. 30:6). Of the Son: 'Truth has sprung from the earth' (Ps. 84:12). And in the Gospel: 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel: 'When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth' (John 16:13). See the unity of the work: do not hesitate to believe the unity of the Trinity. They are also accustomed to say about baptism that their baptism is better than ours, because those who turn from them to us we do not rebaptise, but reconcile by the laying on of hands; whereas they, if they can lead any of ours astray, rebaptise them without consideration. They must be asked: this baptism which they give, do they say it is theirs or ours? If it is ours, why do they take it upon themselves, baptising just as we do? If it is theirs, why do they violate it by repeating it? But we have reverence for the Lord's words, and as he himself commanded, so we baptise: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But it is certain that they too baptise in this way. For if they baptised as they believe, in the name of a greater Father, and in the name of a lesser Son, and in the name of a much lesser Holy Spirit, then indeed we would not be repeating baptism but giving it, because they would not be baptising according to the rule which the Lord handed down. But what do we do? They baptise rightly, but believe wrongly; they baptise rightly, but it is evil that they rebaptise. They baptise according to the rule, but they instil the faith wrongly. And while in a carnal way they make grades in the Godhead, they incur offence against the Godhead, not fearing what the Lord said: 'He who has once been washed does not need to be washed again' (John 13:10). For the Lord said in the Gospel: 'You are the salt of the earth' (Matt. 5:13); and whoever is wise understands that this was not said without reason. For salt is made from water, but if it is put into water again, it dissolves and perishes. So he who has once been baptised from water has been made salt; but if he allows himself to be baptised again, he is reduced to nothing, like salt put into water, and his soul is punished with everlasting death. For the Apostle says of the Church: 'For we, being many, are one bread, one body' (1 Cor. 10:17); because as one loaf is made from many grains, so one Church is gathered from many peoples. And bread, as all know, is made up with water and baked through by fire; and every Christian, through the water of baptism and the fire of the Holy Spirit, has been made an offering to God, as the Lord says: 'Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven' (John 3:5). But just as with bread already once baked, if someone puts it back into water and wishes to mix it again and bake it again, it loses its former worth and turns into blackness and earth, so whoever allows baptism to be repeated on himself becomes such. And therefore each person ought to keep his baptism until death, with God's help, if he wishes to reach the kingdom of heaven faithfully. For whoever allows himself to be rebaptised himself blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, since he denies that he is a Christian and has been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit. And he must necessarily receive that sentence of the threatening Lord which we have mentioned: 'Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come' (Matt. 12:32).
